column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: On the periodic table, what are the vertical columns called?
column28: Vertical columns are groups (older notes also call them families). Horizontal rows are periods.
column29: Vertical means up and down. Which word goes with up-and-down columns, and which goes with side-to-side rows?

column9: Which part of the periodic table indicates the number of energy levels in an atom's electron cloud?
column28: The period (horizontal row) tells the number of energy levels. The group (column, or family) tells the number of valence electrons.
column29: One location tells valence electrons and the other tells energy levels. Which one is the row?

column9: Elements in the same period have the same number of valence electrons.
column28: False. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of energy levels. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons.
column29: Which tells valence electrons: the row or the column?

column9: The elements in Group 18, such as neon and argon, are called the ___.
column20: noble gases|noble gas|the noble gases|noble gasses
column28: Group 18 is the noble gases. They are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable.
column29: This group's name sounds like royalty, and its members are all gases.

column9: Lithium, sodium, and potassium are all in Group 1. What is the name of this group?
column28: Group 1 (not counting hydrogen) is the alkali metals. Alkaline earth metals are Group 2, halogens are Group 17, and noble gases are Group 18.
column29: Group 1 holds the most reactive metals. Which name goes with Group 2, so you can rule it out?

column9: Chlorine (Cl) is in Group 17. How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom have?
column28: For Groups 13–18, take off the 1 in front (skip the transition metals): Group 17 → 7 valence electrons.
column29: Groups 1 and 2 match their number. For Groups 13–18, use the last digit of the group number.

column9: Potassium (K) is in Group 1, Period 4. How many energy levels (shells) does a potassium atom have?
column28: The period number equals the number of energy levels. Period 4 → 4 energy levels.
column29: Which location tells energy levels: the group or the period?

column9: Where are the metals located on the periodic table?
column14: To the left of the staircase line
column15: To the right of the staircase line
column28: Metals are to the left of the metalloids (the staircase line). Nonmetals are to the right, except hydrogen, which sits on the left but is a nonmetal.
column29: Find the staircase line. Most elements are metals, so they take up the bigger side.

column9: Which of these are properties of metals? Select all that apply.
column15: Good conductor of heat and electricity
column28: Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered into sheets), and ductile (can be pulled into wires). Brittle and poor conductors describe nonmetals.
column29: Think of copper wire and aluminum foil. What can you do to them, and what do they carry?

column9: Helium is a noble gas, so it has 8 valence electrons like the rest of Group 18.
column28: False. Helium is the exception in Group 18: it has only 2 electrons total, so it has 2 valence electrons. Its one shell is full with 2.
column29: How many electrons does helium have in all? Can it have more valence electrons than that?

column9: Which of these elements is a metalloid?
column28: Boron is a metalloid. The metalloids sit along the staircase: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te. Carbon and sulfur are nonmetals; sodium is a metal.
column29: Metalloids touch the staircase line. Which choice is right next to it, at the top of the line?

column9: The elements in Group 17, such as fluorine and chlorine, are called the ___.
column28: Group 17 is the halogens, the most reactive nonmetals.
column29: This group holds the most reactive nonmetals. Its name means "salt-former."

column9: The modern periodic table organizes all the known elements by ___.
column16: the year each element was discovered
column28: The periodic table organizes all the elements known to exist by atomic number and chemical properties. Ordering by atomic mass was Mendeleev's first table; Moseley switched it to atomic number.
column29: What number goes up by exactly one from each box to the next?

column9: Hydrogen is in Group 1, but it is not an alkali metal.
column28: True. Hydrogen belongs with the group number (1 valence electron) but not with the group name. It is a nonmetal gas, so it is not an alkali metal.
column29: Is hydrogen a metal or a nonmetal?

column9: Match each group name to how it behaves.
column16: Noble gases :: Nonreactive; already chemically stable
column17: Alkaline earth metals :: Reactive metals with 2 valence electrons
column18: Transition metals :: Skipped when counting valence electrons
column28: Alkali metals are the most reactive metals. Halogens are the most reactive nonmetals. Noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable. Alkaline earth metals have 2 valence electrons. Transition metals (Groups 3–12) are skipped when counting valence electrons.
column29: Two names say "metals" and are reactive; one is the MOST reactive. Which group never reacts?

column9: Gallium (Ga) is in Group 13, Period 4. How many valence electrons does a gallium atom have?
column28: Skip the transition metals: Group 13 → 3 valence electrons. The period (4) tells energy levels, not valence electrons.
column29: For Groups 13–18, drop the 1 in front of the group number.

column9: Selenium (Se) is in Group 16, Period 4. How many valence electrons does a selenium atom have?
column28: Group 16 → 6 valence electrons (skip the transition metals in Groups 3–12). Period 4 would be the number of energy levels.
column29: Valence electrons come from the group, not the period. Then skip Groups 3–12.

column9: Strontium (Sr) is directly below calcium in Group 2. Calcium is in Period 4. How many energy levels does a strontium atom have?
column28: Directly below Period 4 is Period 5, and the period number equals the number of energy levels: 5.
column29: Moving down one box puts you in the next row. Which row is that?

column9: Nitrogen (N) is in Group 15, Period 2. How many valence electrons does a nitrogen atom have?
column28: Group 15 → 5 valence electrons. A common mistake is answering 2, which is the period (energy levels).
column29: Use the group, not the period. Drop the 1 in front of 15.

column9: Calcium (Ca) is in Group 2, Period 4. Which describes a calcium atom?
column28: Group 2 → 2 valence electrons. Period 4 → 4 energy levels. The other choices swap the group and period or use one number twice.
column29: The group gives valence electrons; the period gives energy levels.

column9: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
column14: They have the same number of energy levels
column15: They have the same number of valence electrons
column16: They have the same atomic mass
column17: They have the same number of neutrons
column28: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, and valence electrons decide how an atom reacts. Same energy levels describes a period, not a group.
column29: Which electrons take part in reactions, and what does the group number tell you about them?

column9: Sodium (Group 1, Period 3), calcium (Group 2, Period 4), potassium (Group 1, Period 4), and chlorine (Group 17, Period 3). Which pair would have the most similar chemical properties?
column28: Sodium and potassium are both in Group 1, so both have 1 valence electron and behave alike. Being in the same period (like calcium and potassium, or sodium and chlorine) does not make elements behave alike.
column29: Look for the two elements that share a group, not a period.

column9: Boron, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen have atomic numbers 5, 6, 7, and 8, and each atom has 2 energy levels. They are all members of the same ___.
column28: Same number of energy levels means the same period (row): Period 2. They are in different groups because they have different numbers of valence electrons.
column29: Which location on the table tells the number of energy levels?

column9: Which of these elements are nonmetals? Select all that apply.
column28: Oxygen, sulfur, and neon are nonmetals (right of the staircase). Sodium and iron are metals, and silicon is a metalloid on the staircase.
column29: Nonmetals are right of the staircase line. Watch out for one element that sits ON the line.

column9: Where are the metalloids found on the periodic table?
column14: In Groups 3–12 in the middle of the table
column15: In Group 18 on the far right
column16: Along the staircase line between metals and nonmetals
column17: In the two rows below the main table
column28: The metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit along the stair-step (zig-zag) line between the metals on the left and the nonmetals on the right.
column29: Metalloids are "in between" metals and nonmetals. Where would an in-between group sit?

column9: For nonmetals, reactivity increases as you move down the group.
column28: False. For nonmetals, reactivity decreases as you move down the group. It is metals whose reactivity increases as you move down. That is why fluorine is the most reactive nonmetal.
column29: The most reactive nonmetal, fluorine, is at the top of its group. What does that tell you?

column9: Lithium (Period 2), sodium (Period 3), potassium (Period 4), and cesium (Period 6) are all in Group 1. Which one is the most reactive?
column28: For metals, reactivity increases as you move down the group. Cesium is lowest (Period 6), so it is the most reactive of these.
column29: Do metals get more or less reactive going down a group?

column9: Fluorine (Period 2), chlorine (Period 3), bromine (Period 4), and iodine (Period 5) are all in Group 17. Which one is the most reactive?
column28: For nonmetals, reactivity decreases as you move down the group, so the top one, fluorine, is the most reactive. Fluorine is the most reactive nonmetal on the table.
column29: Halogens are nonmetals. Do nonmetals get more or less reactive going down?

column9: Why do the noble gases not react in nature?
column15: They are already chemically stable with a full outer shell
column16: They are metals, and metals do not react
column17: They have the most protons of any group
column28: Noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable: their outer shell is full. They do have electrons, and they are nonmetals, not metals.
column29: What is special about a noble gas's outermost energy level?

column9: Sample X is a shiny gray solid, but it shatters when hit and conducts electricity only partway (a semi-conductor). Sample X is most likely a ___.
column28: Metalloids are solids with physical properties like metals (shiny) but are semi-conductors and can be brittle. A metal would bend, not shatter; a noble gas is not a solid.
column29: Shiny points one way, brittle points the other. Which class is in between?

column9: Which of these would be the best conductor of electricity?
column28: Silver is a metal, and metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Iodine and argon are nonmetals (poor conductors), and silicon is a metalloid (only a semi-conductor).
column29: Decide which choice is a metal. Metals are the good conductors.

column9: Which of these would be the least reactive?
column28: Argon is a noble gas (Group 18), and noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable. Iodine is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal.
column29: Which choice is in Group 18?

column9: Hydrogen is not an alkali metal. So why is it placed in Group 1?
column15: It is a shiny, soft metal
column16: It has 1 energy level, like all Group 1 elements
column17: It is the most reactive metal
column28: Hydrogen has 1 valence electron, so it belongs with the group number. It does not belong with the group name, because it is a nonmetal gas, not a reactive metal.
column29: What does the group number tell you about an atom's electrons?

column9: Identify the element: I am the alkaline earth metal in Period 3. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: Alkaline earth metals are Group 2. Group 2, Period 3 is magnesium (2 valence electrons, 3 energy levels).
column29: Which group number are the alkaline earth metals? Then go to the third row.

column9: When drawing a Bohr model from an element's spot on the periodic table, which step comes LAST?
column15: Fill electrons from the inside out (2, 8, 8)
column16: Check that the valence electrons match the group number
column28: The last step is a check: the electrons in the outer shell should match the group number (Groups 1, 2, 13–18). You can only check after the shells are filled.
column29: Which step looks back at the finished drawing?

column9: Identify the element: I am a Period 2 nonmetal with 6 valence electrons. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: Period 2 → 2 energy levels. 6 valence electrons → Group 16. Group 16, Period 2 is oxygen.
column29: Turn 6 valence electrons into a group number (add 10). Then find that group in the second row.

column9: Identify the element: I have 6 energy levels and 8 valence electrons. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: 6 energy levels → Period 6. 8 valence electrons → Group 18 (noble gas). Group 18, Period 6 is radon.
column29: Energy levels give the period. 8 valence electrons means the noble gas column.

column9: Identify the element: I am in the same group as bromine (Br), but I have fewer protons than magnesium (atomic number 12).
column28: Bromine is a halogen (Group 17). The only halogen with fewer than 12 protons is fluorine (atomic number 9). Neon has 10 protons but is a noble gas, not in bromine's group.
column29: First name bromine's group. Then check which choice in that group has an atomic number under 12.

column9: Identify the element: I have 3 valence electrons and 4 energy levels.
column28: 3 valence electrons → Group 13. 4 energy levels → Period 4. Gallium is in Group 13, Period 4. Aluminum and boron have 3 valence electrons but fewer energy levels.
column29: Change each clue into a location: valence electrons → group, energy levels → period.

column9: Period 3 contains Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, and Ar. Identify the element: I am the only metalloid in Period 3. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: The metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, and Te. Silicon is the only one in Period 3; aluminum is a metal and phosphorus is a nonmetal.
column29: Find where the staircase line crosses the third row.

column9: Identify the element: I am a metalloid, and my most common isotope has 70 neutrons. Most common isotopes (atomic number): Ge-74 (32), As-75 (33), Sb-121 (51), Te-130 (52).
column29: Subtract the atomic number from each mass number.

column9: Identify the element: I am a shiny solid that conducts electricity well and reacts violently with water. I have 5 energy levels.
column28: Shiny, conducts, and reacts violently with water → an alkali metal (Group 1). 5 energy levels → Period 5. That is rubidium. Potassium is an alkali metal but has only 4 energy levels.
column29: Which group name matches "shiny metal that reacts violently"? Then use the energy levels to pick the row.

column9: An element is in Period 3 and has 5 valence electrons. What is its atomic number?
column28: Period 3 → 3 shells. Fill from the inside out: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 5 in the third (2-8-5). 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 electrons, so 15 protons: atomic number 15 (phosphorus).
column29: Draw the shells: how many shells for Period 3? Fill the inner ones, put the valence electrons on the outside, and add them up.

column9: Neon (Ne) is in Group 18, Period 2. How many valence electrons does a neon atom have?
column28: Group 18 → drop the 1 → 8 valence electrons. Neon has 10 electrons arranged 2-8, so its outer shell holds 8.
column29: For Groups 13–18, drop the 1 in front of the group number.

column9: An element is in Group 2, Period 4. Using shell capacities of 2, 8, 8, how many electrons does a neutral atom of this element have?
column28: Period 4 → 4 shells. Group 2 → 2 valence electrons in the 4th shell. Fill the inner shells: 2-8-8-2. 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 = 20 electrons (calcium).
column29: Fill the inner shells completely, then put the group's valence electrons in the outer shell. Add them up.

column9: An element is in Group 14, Period 3. Which electron arrangement does it have?
column28: Period 3 → 3 shells. Group 14 → 4 valence electrons. Fill from the inside out: 2-8-4 (silicon). 4-8-2 fills from the outside in, 2-4 has only 2 shells, and 2-8-8-4 has 4 shells.
column29: Count the shells from the period, put the valence electrons in the last shell, and fill inside out.

column9: An atom's electrons are arranged 2-8-7. Where is this element on the periodic table?
column28: 3 shells → Period 3. 7 valence electrons → Group 17 (skip the transition metals). Group 17, Period 3 is chlorine.
column29: The number of shells gives the period. The electrons in the last shell give the group (for 3 to 8 valence electrons, add 10).

column9: Jae says, "Iron (Fe) is in Group 8, so it has 8 valence electrons." Which response is best?
column14: He is right; valence electrons always equal the group number
column15: He is wrong; the valence rule skips the transition metals in Groups 3–12
column16: He is wrong; iron would have 18 valence electrons
column17: He is wrong; the period number tells valence electrons, not the group
column28: Jae is wrong. Groups 3–12 are transition metals, and the valence rule skips them. It only works for Groups 1, 2, and 13–18 (Group 18 = 8, except helium).
column29: Which groups does the valence electron rule work for?

column9: Sodium (Group 1, Period 3) and chlorine (Group 17, Period 3) have similar chemical properties because they are in the same period.
column28: False. Being in the same period only means the same number of energy levels. Sodium has 1 valence electron (reactive metal) and chlorine has 7 (reactive nonmetal), so they behave very differently.
column29: Similar properties come from having the same number of what? Do sodium and chlorine share that?

column9: Beryllium (atomic number 4), magnesium (12), strontium (38), and barium (56) are all in Group 2. Put them in order from least reactive to most reactive.
column28: Higher atomic number means lower in the group. For metals, reactivity increases as you move down the group: Be, Mg, Sr, Ba (least to most reactive).
column29: Use atomic number to decide which is lowest in the group. Do metals get more reactive going down?

column9: How many periods (horizontal rows) does the periodic table have?
column28: The periodic table has 7 periods. The period number tells how many energy levels an atom has, so there are 7 possible numbers of energy levels. It has 18 groups (columns).
column29: Count the rows on the main table, not the columns.

column9: What is another name for a group (vertical column) on the periodic table?
column28: Groups are also called families, because the elements in a column behave alike, like members of a family. Periods are the rows.
column29: Elements in a column are related, like relatives.

column9: How many valence electrons does an atom in Group 2, such as magnesium, have?
column28: Groups 1 and 2 match their number of valence electrons, so Group 2 → 2 valence electrons.
column29: For Groups 1 and 2, the group number is the answer.

column9: Carbon sits in Group 14. Using the skip-the-transition-metals rule, how many valence electrons does carbon have?
column28: Skip Groups 3–12 (the transition metals): Group 13 = 3, so Group 14 = 4 valence electrons. Carbon's arrangement is 2-4, with 4 in the outer shell.
column29: For Groups 13–18, drop the 1 in front of the group number.

column9: Lithium is the first metal in Group 1. How many valence electrons does a lithium atom have?
column28: Group 1 → 1 valence electron. Lithium's arrangement is 2-1, so it has 1 electron in its outer shell.
column29: The group number matches the valence electrons for Groups 1 and 2.

column9: Xenon (Xe) is in Period 5. How many energy levels does a xenon atom have?
column28: The period number equals the number of energy levels, so Period 5 → 5 energy levels.
column29: Which location tells energy levels: the row or the column?

column9: Oxygen is in Group 16 and Period 2. Which description of an oxygen atom is correct?
column28: Group 16 → skip the transition metals → 6 valence electrons. Period 2 → 2 energy levels. Its arrangement is 2-6.
column29: The group gives valence electrons; the period gives energy levels.

column9: What are the elements in Group 2 called?
column28: Group 2 is the alkaline earth metals. Group 1 is the alkali metals, Group 17 is the halogens, and Groups 3–12 are the transition metals.
column29: The name sounds a lot like the Group 1 name, with one extra word.

column9: Which groups hold the transition metals?
column28: The transition metals are Groups 3–12, the wide middle section of the table. That is why the valence electron rule skips those groups.
column29: Think of the big block in the middle of the table.

column9: A sample is a dull yellow solid. It crumbles when you hit it, and it does not conduct electricity. What is it most likely to be?
column28: Dull, brittle, and a poor conductor are the properties of a nonmetal (this sample is sulfur). A metal would be shiny, bend instead of crumbling, and conduct well.
column29: Is it shiny? Does it bend or break? Does it conduct?

column9: Look at where each element sits compared to the staircase line. Which ones are metalloids? Select all that apply.
column28: The metalloids sit along the staircase line: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, and Te. Silicon, germanium, and arsenic are metalloids. Carbon and phosphorus are nonmetals, and aluminum is a metal.
column29: Find each element on the table. Does it touch the staircase line?

column9: Mr. Erickson's reactivity rule: going down a group of METALS (like Group 1), reactivity ___.
column20: increases|goes up|increase|rises|gets higher|gets bigger|grows|gets stronger|gets greater|goes higher
column28: For metals, reactivity increases as you move down a group, so cesium is more reactive than sodium. For nonmetals it is the opposite: reactivity decreases going down.
column29: Think about the reactivity lab: which was more reactive, magnesium or calcium, and which one is lower in Group 2?

column9: Chlorine and bromine are both halogens, and bromine is directly below chlorine. Which one is more reactive?
column14: Chlorine, because nonmetals get less reactive going down a group
column15: Bromine, because it is lower in the group
column16: They are equally reactive, because they are in the same group
column17: Bromine, because it has more protons
column28: Halogens are nonmetals, and for nonmetals reactivity decreases going down a group. Chlorine is higher, so chlorine is more reactive. (For metals the trend goes the other way.)
column29: Do nonmetals get more or less reactive going down a group?

column9: Which element is in Group 1, Period 3?
column28: Group 1, Period 3 is sodium (Na): 1 valence electron and 3 energy levels. Lithium is Period 2, potassium is Period 4, and magnesium is Group 2.
column29: Go to the first column, then down to the third row.

column9: Which element is the noble gas in Period 3?
column28: Noble gases are Group 18. Group 18, Period 3 is argon. Neon is in Period 2, krypton is in Period 4, and chlorine is a halogen.
column29: Noble gases are in the last column. Which one is in the third row?

column9: Potassium is directly below sodium in Group 1. A potassium atom has more energy levels than a sodium atom.
column28: True. Moving down one box puts you in the next period. Sodium is in Period 3 (3 energy levels) and potassium is in Period 4 (4 energy levels). They have the same number of valence electrons, because they share a group.
column29: Which location tells energy levels: the column or the row?

column9: Aluminum is in Group 13. Why does it have 3 valence electrons instead of 13?
column14: You skip the transition metals in Groups 3–12
column16: You subtract the period number from the group number
column17: It is a mistake on the periodic table
column28: The valence rule skips the 10 transition metal groups (3–12), so Group 13 → 3 valence electrons. Aluminum's arrangement, 2-8-3, shows 3 electrons in its outer shell.
column29: Which groups do you skip when you count valence electrons?

column9: Which element has 2 energy levels and 1 valence electron?
column28: 2 energy levels → Period 2. 1 valence electron → Group 1. Group 1, Period 2 is lithium. Sodium has 3 energy levels, beryllium has 2 valence electrons, and hydrogen has only 1 energy level.
column29: Turn each clue into a location: energy levels → period, valence electrons → group.

column9: Which element would react most like nitrogen?
column28: Phosphorus is directly below nitrogen in Group 15, so both have 5 valence electrons and similar chemical properties. Oxygen, carbon, and neon are in the same period as nitrogen, not the same group.
column29: Elements in the same column behave alike. Which one is in nitrogen's column?

column9: Most of the elements on the periodic table are...
column28: Metals take up the whole left side and middle of the table, so most elements are metals. Nonmetals are on the right, and metalloids are only the few along the staircase line.
column29: Which side of the staircase line is bigger?

column9: Metalloids have physical properties like ___ and chemical properties like ___.
column28: Metalloids sit between metals and nonmetals. They look and act physically like metals (for example, some are shiny solids) but react chemically like nonmetals, and they are semiconductors.
column29: Metalloids are in-between elements. Which properties do you see, and which show up in reactions?

column9: Beryllium is in Group 2 and Period 2. Which electron arrangement does a neutral beryllium atom have?
column28: Period 2 → 2 shells. Group 2 → 2 valence electrons in the outer shell. Fill inside out: 2-2 (4 electrons total). 2-8-2 would need a third shell.
column29: Count the shells from the period, then put the group's valence electrons in the last shell.

column9: Nickel, calcium, sulfur, and argon: which one belongs to the transition metals?
column28: Nickel is in Group 10, in the middle block (Groups 3–12), so it is a transition metal. Calcium is an alkaline earth metal, sulfur is a nonmetal, and argon is a noble gas.
column29: Which element is in the middle block of the table?

column9: Electric wires are made of good conductors. Which of these elements would make the WORST wire, because it is the poorest conductor of electricity?
column28: Sulfur is a nonmetal, and nonmetals are poor conductors. Copper, aluminum, and iron are metals, which are good conductors of heat and electricity.
column29: Three of these are metals. Which one is not?

column9: Which element has 7 valence electrons?
column28: Iodine is in Group 17 (a halogen), so it has 7 valence electrons. Nitrogen (Group 15) has 5, oxygen (Group 16) has 6, and neon (Group 18) has 8.
column29: 7 valence electrons means Group 17. Which choice is a halogen?

column9: Oxygen, sulfur, selenium, and tellurium are all in Group 16. Which one has the MOST energy levels?
column28: Tellurium is lowest in the group (Period 5), so it has 5 energy levels. Oxygen (Period 2), sulfur (Period 3), and selenium (Period 4) have fewer.
column29: Energy levels come from the period. Which element is lowest in the column?

column9: A student is sorting six elements into metals and nonmetals. Which elements belong in the metals pile? Select all that apply.
column28: Sodium, iron, and calcium are left of the staircase line, so they are metals. Sulfur and neon are nonmetals, and silicon is a metalloid on the staircase.
column29: Metals are left of the staircase line. Watch out for an element that sits ON the line.

column9: Counting from left to right, how many groups (columns) are on the periodic table?
column28: The periodic table has 18 groups, numbered 1 to 18 from left to right. It has 7 periods (rows).
column29: The noble gases are in the very last column. What is that column's number?

column9: Which halogen has 3 energy levels?
column28: Halogens are Group 17, and 3 energy levels means Period 3. Group 17, Period 3 is chlorine. Fluorine has 2 energy levels and bromine has 4. Argon has 3 energy levels but is a noble gas.
column29: Halogen → which group? 3 energy levels → which period?

column9: An atom has 3 energy levels and 2 valence electrons. Which element is it?
column28: 3 energy levels → Period 3. 2 valence electrons → Group 2. Group 2, Period 3 is magnesium (2-8-2). Calcium has 4 energy levels, beryllium has 2, and aluminum has 3 valence electrons.
column29: Turn the clues into a period and a group.

column9: An element is in Group 17, Period 2. Using shell capacities of 2, 8, 8, what is its atomic number?
column28: Period 2 → 2 shells. Group 17 → 7 valence electrons in the outer shell. Fill inside out: 2-7, which is 9 electrons, so 9 protons: atomic number 9 (fluorine).
column29: Draw the shells: fill the inner shell, put the valence electrons in the outer shell, and add.

column9: Identify the element: I am a metalloid in Period 4, and I have 4 valence electrons.
column28: 4 valence electrons → Group 14. Period 4, Group 14 is germanium, a metalloid on the staircase. Silicon is in Period 3, arsenic has 5 valence electrons, and tin is in Period 5.
column29: Change the valence electrons into a group, then go to the fourth row.

column9: Put these halogens in order from LEAST reactive to MOST reactive.
column28: Halogens are nonmetals, so reactivity decreases going down the group. From the bottom up: iodine (Period 5), bromine (Period 4), chlorine (Period 3), fluorine (Period 2), the most reactive nonmetal.
column29: For nonmetals, the element at the top of the group is the most reactive.

column9: Which pair of elements has the SAME number of valence electrons?
column28: Oxygen and selenium are both in Group 16, so each has 6 valence electrons. The other pairs are in different groups: oxygen and fluorine (6 and 7), sodium and neon (1 and 8), carbon and nitrogen (4 and 5).
column29: Same number of valence electrons means the same group.

column9: Which two elements are in the same period, so their atoms have the same number of energy levels?
column28: Lithium and fluorine are both in Period 2, so each has 2 energy levels. Lithium and sodium are in the same group, not period, and so are fluorine and chlorine.
column29: Same number of energy levels means the same row.

column9: Sodium reacts strongly with water. Which of these elements would most likely also react strongly with water?
column28: Lithium is in Group 1 with sodium, so it has the same number of valence electrons (1) and similar chemical properties. Neon is a nonreactive noble gas, sulfur is a nonmetal, and aluminum is in a different group.
column29: Which element is in sodium's family?

column9: Silicon is used to make computer chips. Which property of metalloids makes them useful for this?
column14: They are semiconductors that conduct electricity only partway
column15: They are the best conductors of all the elements
column16: They are gases at room temperature
column17: They are the most reactive elements
column28: Metalloids are semiconductors: they conduct electricity only partway, which lets chips control electric current. They are solids, not gases, and they are not the best conductors (metals are).
column29: Metalloids are in between metals and nonmetals. How well do they conduct?

column9: Using shell capacities of 2, 8, 8, how many electrons does a neutral atom of the element in Group 13, Period 2 have?
column28: Period 2 → 2 shells. Group 13 → 3 valence electrons. Fill inside out: 2-3, so 2 + 3 = 5 electrons (boron).
column29: Fill the inner shell completely, then put the valence electrons in the outer shell. Add them up.

column9: Ava says, "Magnesium is in Group 2, so it has 2 energy levels." Which response is correct?
column14: She is right; the group number is the number of energy levels.
column15: She is wrong; magnesium has 12 energy levels.
column16: She is wrong; the period tells energy levels, and magnesium is in Period 3, so it has 3.
column17: She is wrong; magnesium has no energy levels because it is a metal.
column28: The group tells valence electrons and the period tells energy levels. Magnesium is in Group 2 (2 valence electrons) and Period 3, so it has 3 energy levels (2-8-2).
column29: Which location tells energy levels: the group or the period?

column9: Which statements about the alkali metals are true? Select all that apply.
column16: They get more reactive going down the group
column17: Hydrogen is one of the alkali metals
column18: They are nonreactive, like the noble gases
column28: The alkali metals are Group 1, each with 1 valence electron, and they get more reactive going down the group. Hydrogen sits in Group 1 but is a nonmetal, not an alkali metal, and the alkali metals are the most reactive metals, not nonreactive.
column29: Think about their group number, valence electrons, and the metal reactivity trend.

column9: Identify the element: I am in the same period as sodium and in the same group as oxygen.
column28: Sodium is in Period 3, and oxygen is in Group 16. Period 3, Group 16 is sulfur. Selenium is in Group 16 but Period 4, chlorine is in Group 17, and magnesium is in Group 2.
column29: Find sodium's period and oxygen's group, then find where they cross.

column9: Identify the element: I am a halogen with more energy levels than chlorine but fewer energy levels than iodine.
column28: Chlorine is in Period 3 and iodine is in Period 5, so this halogen is in Period 4: bromine. Krypton is in Period 4 too, but it is a noble gas, not a halogen.
column29: Find the periods of chlorine and iodine. Which period is in between?

column9: A neutral atom's electrons are arranged 2-8-6. What group number is this element in?
column28: The outer shell holds 6 valence electrons. For 3 to 8 valence electrons, add 10 to get the group (skipping the transition metals): Group 16. It has 3 shells, so it is in Period 3: sulfur.
column29: Valence electrons are in the last shell. How do you turn 6 valence electrons into a group number?

column9: Which statement correctly compares the reactivity trends for metals and nonmetals?
column14: Both metals and nonmetals get more reactive going down a group
column15: Both metals and nonmetals get less reactive going down a group
column16: Metals get less reactive going down a group, and nonmetals get more reactive
column17: Metals get more reactive going down a group, and nonmetals get less reactive
column28: Metals get MORE reactive going down a group (cesium is more reactive than lithium). Nonmetals get LESS reactive going down a group (fluorine is more reactive than iodine). The trends run in opposite directions.
column29: Where is the most reactive alkali metal, and where is the most reactive halogen?

column9: Jae says, "Fluorine is at the top of its group, so it is the LEAST reactive halogen, just like lithium is the least reactive alkali metal." Which response is best?
column15: He is right about lithium but wrong about fluorine; fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
column16: He is wrong about lithium, but right about fluorine.
column17: He is wrong about both; position in a group has nothing to do with reactivity.
column28: Jae is right about lithium: for metals, reactivity increases going down, so the top metal is the least reactive. But for nonmetals the trend is reversed, so fluorine, at the top of Group 17, is the MOST reactive halogen.
column29: Do metals and nonmetals follow the same reactivity trend?

column9: An element is in Group 14, Period 2. Which statements about it are true? Select all that apply.
column28: Group 14 → 4 valence electrons. Period 2 → 2 energy levels. Fill inside out: 2-4. Group 14, Period 2 is carbon, which is right of the staircase, so it is a nonmetal. It is not a metalloid, and it does not have 14 valence electrons.
column29: Work out the valence electrons, the energy levels, and the arrangement, then find the element.

column9: Element X is in the same period as lithium and has 4 more valence electrons than lithium. What is the atomic number of element X?
column28: Lithium is in Period 2 with 1 valence electron, so X is in Period 2 with 1 + 4 = 5 valence electrons (Group 15). Its arrangement is 2-5, which is 7 electrons, so its atomic number is 7 (nitrogen).
column29: Find lithium's period and valence electrons first, then build X's arrangement.

column9: Element Z is in the same group as neon. Which statement about element Z is most likely true?
column14: It is nonreactive because its outer shell is full
column28: Neon is a noble gas (Group 18). Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they are already chemically stable and nonreactive. Shiny metals that react violently are alkali metals, which have 1 valence electron.
column29: Which group is neon in, and how do the elements in that group behave?

column9: An unknown element is a gas at room temperature, does not conduct electricity, and reacts with almost nothing. Where on the periodic table is it most likely found?
column28: A nonreactive gas that does not conduct is a noble gas: Group 18, on the far right. Group 1 holds very reactive metals, Groups 3–12 are metals, and the staircase line holds solid metalloids.
column29: Which family is nonreactive?

column9: An element in Period 3 has an outer shell that is exactly half full, if a full outer shell holds 8 electrons. What is its atomic number?
column28: Half of 8 is 4, so the outer shell has 4 valence electrons (Group 14). Period 3 means 3 shells: 2-8-4. 2 + 8 + 4 = 14 electrons, so the atomic number is 14 (silicon).
column29: How many valence electrons is half full? Then fill the inner shells and add.
